questions.q: Per this lesson, why does an undocumented tradeoff decision become a liability once the original architect leaves the project?
options: It isn't actually a liability -- documentation is purely a bureaucratic formality with no real cost to skipping it
Salesforce automatically reverts undocumented decisions after the architect leaves
Undocumented decisions are illegal under Salesforce's terms of service

A new team member has no way to tell whether the existing choice was a deliberate, reasoned decision or an accident, leaving only the bad options of trusting it blindly or re-litigating it from scratch
questions.explain: Without a record, every past decision looks equally arbitrary to someone new, which forces a bad choice between blind trust and re-litigating the decision from scratch -- exactly what a short, honest writeup would have prevented.

questions.q: What are the five parts of a good Architecture Decision Record (ADR) as described in this lesson?
options: Context, options considered, decision, rationale (naming what was traded away), and conditions for revisiting
Budget, timeline, stakeholders, risks, and sign-off
Requirements, design, implementation, testing, and deployment
Problem, solution, code, tests, and documentation
questions.explain: This five-part structure captures the constraints that made it a real decision, the realistic alternatives, the plain decision itself, the honest cost of the choice, and what would trigger revisiting it later.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the 'rationale' section is the most important, and most often skipped, part of an ADR?
options: Because it should only ever praise the chosen option, with no mention of any downside
Because naming the specific cost that was traded away, not just the benefit gained, is what makes the record honest and genuinely useful to a future reader
Because it's the only section that requires a manager's signature
Because it is the longest section and therefore the most time-consuming to write
questions.explain: A rationale that says only 'we chose Flow for maintainability' omits the cost; naming what was given up (for example, a cap on how complex the branching logic can get) is what lets a future reader actually evaluate whether the tradeoff still holds.

questions.q: What does this lesson say is wrong with a vague ADR rationale like 'we chose the best option for scalability'?
options: Nothing -- vague language is preferred because it keeps the record flexible
It is too long and should be shortened further
It gives a false sense that reasoning happened without actually preserving any of the specific reasoning a future reader would need
It violates Salesforce's AppExchange security review requirements
questions.explain: The lesson calls vague language worse than useless for exactly this reason -- it looks like documentation without actually recording anything a future reader could check or act on.

questions.q: How does this lesson say documented tradeoffs connect to later skills in this course, such as explaining tradeoffs to executives or running a review board?
options: They are unrelated -- documentation is a separate skill from executive communication
Review boards are required to reject any decision that has an ADR
ADRs replace the need for any live executive conversation entirely
Having the reasoning already written down makes those later conversations dramatically easier, since an ADR already answers the 'why not the other option' question an audience is likely to ask
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames ADRs as groundwork for Chapter 3's executive-communication and review-board skills -- reconstructing reasoning live, under pressure, is much harder than presenting from a record that already exists.
